A beginner can start with the three parts of a Rio carnival bateria: the largest and lowest plays the second beat of the basic “first beat, second beat” and sets the pulse; the slightly smaller drum plays the first beat; the smallest plays syncopation and fills and is the part with most room to improvise. The surdo is a Brazilian membranophone, Hornbostel–Sachs number 211.212.11, a large bass drum or floor drum about 40–65 cm across, with some at 73 cm. The shell may be wood, galvanised steel or aluminium and the head goatskin or plastic; the player hangs it from a belt or shoulder strap with the head roughly level, strikes only the upper head, and uses hard or soft sticks. It was created by Alcebíades Barcelos in the 1920s–1930s through his contribution to Deixa Falar, the first samba school in Rio de Janeiro, and is used by samba-school baterias, axé / samba-reggae groups in northeastern Brazil and small samba and pagode groups, where it carries the bass pulse.
蘇爾多低音鼓音色低沉厚實，具有深邃而暗沉的質感。其音域位於打擊樂器的最低層，能發: The surdo's tone is deep and thick, with a dark, profound quality. Its range is the lowest layer of the percussion, and it produces a strong low-frequency resonance that lays a firm rhythmic foundation for the whole band. Its way of resonating, through the vibration of the head, is distinctive, and it can be felt physically in the air. Compared with the sharp clarity of the high drums, the surdo's sound wraps around you and carries further; it is like the bass drum of the Western orchestra, but thicker and warmer. Different sizes differ noticeably in timbre: smaller drums sit relatively higher, larger ones are deeper and more powerful, and in a Brazilian samba band they combine with the other percussion into richly layered harmony.
